title: The Fight Over Ratification
objective: After this level you can compare the Federalists' and Anti-Federalists' arguments, and explain how their fight produced the Bill of Rights.
summary: Federalists wrote The Federalist to win ratification; Anti-Federalists feared a distant national government with no bill of rights. Their fight produced the Bill of Rights in 1791.

cards.headline: The Constitution’s fiercest critics ended up improving it.
cards.body: Opponents said it lacked a bill of rights. Supporters said it didn’t need one. Their fight produced the first 10 amendments.

cards.headline: The case for
cards.body: Supporters of the Constitution called themselves Federalists. To win over New York, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote The Federalist: 85 essays printed in New York newspapers from October 1787 to May 1788. They were newspaper columns long before they were a classic.

cards.headline: The case against
cards.body: Anti-Federalists, including Patrick Henry, feared the plan. A single national government, they warned, could bring upper-class dominance, weak separation of powers and the loss of local control. George Mason, a delegate to the convention itself, refused to sign because the Constitution lacked a bill of rights.

cards.headline: A deal in Massachusetts
cards.body: Federalists first argued a bill of rights was unnecessary: the new government could use only the powers the Constitution listed. But with ratification in danger in Massachusetts, they agreed that the First Congress would consider amendments proposed by the states. That promise secured ratification there.

cards.headline: The losers write a chapter
cards.body: James Madison, who had once opposed a bill of rights, introduced a list of amendments in the First Congress on June 8, 1789. Congress proposed 12, and by December 15, 1791, the states had ratified 10: the Bill of Rights. The Anti-Federalists lost the fight, but their agitation added the Bill of Rights.

cards.headline: The Fight Over Ratification: explained
learned: Federalists: The Federalist, 85 essays by Hamilton, Madison and Jay
Anti-Federalists: feared a distant national government
Massachusetts ratified after Federalists promised amendments
Madison’s amendments became the Bill of Rights in 1791

questions.prompt: Match each person, group or writing with its part in the ratification fight.
questions.explanation: The Federalist was 85 essays, George Mason refused to sign, the Anti-Federalists warned of upper-class dominance, and James Madison introduced a list of amendments in the First Congress.

questions.prompt: How did the ratification fight lead to the Bill of Rights?

options.label: The Federalist essays demanded 10 amendments
options.rationale: Federalists first called a bill of rights unnecessary.

options.label: Anti-Federalists wrote it into the Philadelphia draft
options.rationale: It came later, in the First Congress.

options.label: Federalists promised amendments to win ratification
Britain demanded it in a treaty
options.rationale: It came from an American political deal.

questions.explanation: To secure ratification, Federalists promised amendments; Madison introduced them in 1789.

questions.prompt: Anti-Federalists feared a strong national government. Yet the Articles of Confederation showed the risk of a weak one. What couldn’t the Articles’ Congress do?

options.label: Make the states pay what it requested
Request troops from the thirteen states
options.rationale: It could request them, but not enforce the request.

options.label: Meet at all during the 1780s
options.rationale: It met; it just couldn’t enforce its requests.

questions.explanation: Congress could request money and troops but had no power to make the states pay.
